facts.claim: "Raising Hell" is track 6 (3:32) on Lucero's self-titled debut album, released May 22, 2001.
The album was recorded by Kevin Houston on March 28 1999, September 29 1999 and May 5 2000 at the Dickinson family's barn in Coldwater, Mississippi.
The album was mixed by Kevin Houston at Sounds Unreel in Memphis and mastered by Brad Blackwood at Ardent in Memphis.
The album was produced by Cody Dickinson and Lucero.

The lineup on the album was Brian Venable (guitar), Ben Nichols (vocals, guitar), Roy Berry (drums) and John C. Stubblefield (bass). Luther Dickinson (lap steel, mandolin, guitar), Cody Dickinson (guitar, pump organ, Moog) and East Memphis Slim (piano, Wurlitzer organ) also played on it.
Streaming metadata credits Ben Nichols as the composer of "Raising Hell".
Ben Nichols says the band recorded its first two records, the self-titled album and Tennessee, with Cody Dickinson at the barn in Coldwater, Mississippi.

For the album's 20th anniversary, Nichols said he is very proud of the self-titled record and that it shows where Lucero was heading. At that point his idea of what the band should be was still coming together.
The album was first issued on CD by Madjack Records. Liberty & Lament put out a 2xLP edition on February 25, 2022, the first time it was pressed on vinyl.
Lucero is a Memphis band formed by Ben Nichols in the late 1990s. It first played in early 1998 and takes its name from the Spanish word for "bright star".

research.lineage: Lucero sits in Memphis-rooted alt-country and country-punk, mixing punk-rock energy with Southern roots music and early rock and roll.

draft:
**Raising Hell** opens on a brag that's really a worry. "Well my little brother's raising hell," Ben Nichols sings, and the next lines pile up the evidence: whiskey nights, rodeos, strippers in Austin, a kid who probably ought to be in jail and can't remember the good times he keeps telling everyone about. There's pride in the telling, the way an older sibling passes along the wild stories at the dinner table. There's also worry, because the brother's money is running out and a job is the one option he won't consider.

Then Nichols, who wrote the song, turns to someone else. The second verse belongs to a "you" in a house where winter is cold and wet at once and the roof leaks. "Make keeping dry a losing game" is the line doing the work: a practical complaint that is plainly about crying too. Her boy is coming home and it won't help. The narrator tells her to dry her eyes and let him go. The song never says whether he speaks as a friend or as the boy himself, and the tenderness holds either way.

The last portrait is his own, and it's the least flattering. It's the same old weight pulling him down and the same big plans always in the works, with a bet that they'll pay off before his luck gives out. He admits he doesn't know if he's right, then digs in: "but i can tell you that i'm having fun." That line holds the song's mix of self-defense and ache. Fun is the alibi. All three people end up facing the same choice of where to run, and he chooses running itself. Then the lyric circles back to the brother in Texas, as if the whole cycle starts over.

The band plays it easy. A clean electric guitar picks out arpeggiated chords, the bass walks underneath, and the drums keep a steady, relaxed mid-tempo. Nichols sings in the middle of his range, raw and unvarnished, and a second voice slips in to harmonize on some phrases. The room sounds natural, like a band standing in one space. That fits, since Kevin Houston recorded the album in the Dickinson family's barn in Coldwater, Mississippi, across sessions in 1999 and 2000, with Cody Dickinson and Lucero producing. This is Memphis alt-country with punk still under its fingernails, though here the volume is down and the storytelling is up front. Nichols has said the debut shows where Lucero was heading. You can hear it in this song's character sketches, its shrug, and the hurt underneath.

The song sticks because it lets you feel proud of the people you love and scared for them in the same breath, and it counts the singer among them.
